subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Project log, site 14. Written by Vidya Kulkarni, project head. On Tuesday the contractor wanted the night crew up on the scaffolds during the storm warning. It was within the permit, and the crew leader said his men needed the overtime. Pranav, our junior site engineer, refused to sign the shift sheet. He said, "The permit allows it, but I won't send people up where I wouldn't go myself. Their lives aren't worth less because they are paid by the day." The contractor complained to head office, and Pranav lost his quarterly bonus for delaying the pour. He knew that would happen and did not argue the penalty. I don't think Pranav is some kind of saint; last month he rushed his paperwork like everyone else. But on Tuesday he held a line on principle. I have asked head office to review storm permits.

qa.q: What did the contractor want the night crew to do on Tuesday?
qa.a: To be up on the scaffolds during the storm warning.

qa.q: What did Pranav feel about the day-paid workers, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt protective of them, believing their lives were worth no less than anyone's; he said he wouldn't send people up where he wouldn't go himself.

qa.q: What choice did Vidya make after Tuesday, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Vidya asked head office to review storm permits, which could turn one person's stand into a safer rule for every crew.

qa.q: How might the crew leader see Pranav's refusal?
qa.a: The crew leader may be torn: relieved the men stayed safe, yet frustrated that they lost overtime they needed.

grounding: A young engineer acts on a principle of human dignity against a permit and the contractor's wishes and accepts losing his bonus, while the note shows he is not always at that level.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: Wednesday night. Today I said no to Deepak for the first time. The flood pictures came in: a mother on a rooftop holding her child's slipper, her face clear, crying. Deepak wanted it for the front page. It is legal; the photographer shot it in a public place, and the whole desk agreed it would sell. I kept thinking: she never agreed to become the face of this. Her grief isn't ours to use. I asked for the picture of the water and the empty street instead. Deepak said I'd lost my nerve and took me off the flood series. That stung more than I expected. I'm no hero; most days I just go along with the desk. But tonight I know exactly why I said no, and I would say it again. - Vikas

qa.q: What did Vikas ask for instead of the mother's picture?
qa.a: The picture of the water and the empty street.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel while looking at the flood picture?
qa.a: Vikas felt uneasy about using it, thinking the mother never agreed to become the face of the story and her grief wasn't theirs to use.

qa.q: What choice did Vikas make, and what did it cost?
qa.a: Vikas refused to run the mother's photo and offered another, and the cost was being taken off the flood series.

qa.q: How might the mother in the photograph have been affected if the picture had run on the front page?
qa.a: Her private grief would have become a public image without her consent, at one of the worst moments of her life.

grounding: A young journalist acts on a self-chosen principle of dignity against the law's permission and the desk's wishes, accepts the cost, and admits it is not how they usually act.

passage:
When Dolma's son was arrested in town, the village council in Kaza decided her family would not draw from the common tap until the case was over. "We don't want trouble here," the headman said. No one argued.
Sahil, twenty-five, taught at the village school. Next morning he walked with Dolma to the tap, filled her two cans, and carried one home for her. At the council he said, "Her grandson is in my class. He is not accused of anything. Nor is she. Water is not a reward for good behaviour."
The council fined him, and his landlord asked him to find another room. He paid, packed, and moved into a draughty storeroom behind the school.
He was no saint about it. At night he lay awake wondering whether his mother would be ashamed of the gossip, and whether he had been proud rather than right. In the morning he carried the cans again.

qa.q: What did the village council decide about Dolma's family?
qa.a: It decided her family would not draw from the common tap until the case was over.

qa.q: What was Sahil worried about at night, even while he kept carrying the cans?
qa.a: He worried his mother would be ashamed of the gossip, and whether he had been proud rather than right.

qa.q: What was Sahil's turning-point choice, and what did it cost him?
qa.a: He chose to fetch water with Dolma openly and tell the council why, and it cost him a fine and his room.

qa.q: How might Dolma's grandson see Sahil after this?
qa.a: He might see his teacher as someone who treated his family as people when the village turned away, and that could stay with him a long time. 🤍

grounding: A young teacher acts on his own principle of dignity against the village council's ban, accepts the fine and loss of his room, and still doubts himself.

passage:
The council notice on the park railings in Nairobi was new: no food handouts without a permit, and a fine for anyone who ignored it. The permit list had a two-year wait.
Wanjiru, twenty-six, had shared her lunch there with the same three street boys every Friday for a year. Her flatmate Mina read the notice aloud. "You'll get fined. People at your office already think you're mad."
"They're children, Mina. I'm not going to make them watch me eat."
On Friday an officer wrote her the fine. Wanjiru paid it that afternoon and that night wrote to her ward councillor asking for a simple permit for small, one-person sharing.
Mina teased her about being a saint. Wanjiru laughed. "Saints don't check their bank balance twice after a fine. Most days I follow rules just to stay out of trouble, like everyone."

qa.q: How long was the wait on the permit list?
qa.a: The permit list had a two-year wait.

qa.q: Why did Wanjiru keep sharing her lunch after the notice went up?
qa.a: She felt protective of the boys and cared more that children shouldn't have to watch her eat than about the fine or her office's opinion.

qa.q: Besides paying the fine, what step did Wanjiru take, and why is it a sensible choice?
qa.a: She wrote to her ward councillor asking for a simple permit for small sharing, which works to change the rule rather than only defying it.

qa.q: How does Mina's view of Wanjiru's choice differ from Wanjiru's own?
qa.a: Mina sees risk and a reputation for being mad and jokes about sainthood, while Wanjiru sees an ordinary person who mostly follows rules but won't bend on this one.

grounding: A young woman acts on her principle of human dignity against a feeding by-law, accepts the fine, and admits that most days she follows rules like anyone.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Beatriz, twenty-six, taught at a primary school in Recife. In March the district office sent a notice: children without complete papers could no longer attend until the paperwork was done. It could take months.
Yara, eight, was one of them. Her family had fled another country. She was the best reader in the class.
Colleagues said, "It's the rule. We'll get in trouble."
Beatriz thought about it for two nights. Then she decided: a child's right to learn and her dignity mattered more to her than the notice. She kept Yara in her classroom, openly, and wrote to the district explaining why.
She got a formal warning. Some colleagues stopped sitting with her at lunch.
She accepted it. "I know most people wouldn't do this," she told her sister. "I'm not sure I always would. But this time I had to."

qa.q: How old was Yara?
qa.a: Eight.

qa.q: What was Beatriz feeling during the two nights she thought about it?
qa.a: She felt torn and uneasy, weighing the rule against Yara's right to learn.

qa.q: What did Beatriz do, and what did it cost her?
qa.a: She kept Yara in class openly and wrote to the district explaining why; she got a formal warning and some colleagues withdrew.

qa.q: How might Yara feel being allowed to stay?
qa.a: She would probably feel safe and valued, able to keep learning and reading in her class.

grounding: It shows an adult acting on self-chosen principles of dignity even against a rule and colleagues, accepting the cost, and noting it is rare.

passage:
At the chemical plant office, the quarterly safety report was due. Mohit, twenty-five, noticed that two leak readings from the east unit had been left out.
His team lead, Hrithik, said, "Everyone does this. If we include them, the plant gets inspected, the bonus goes, and the whole team suffers."
The team nodded. Nobody wanted trouble.
Mohit went home and couldn't eat. The villagers downstream used the canal water. That thought wouldn't leave him.
The next morning he told Hrithik, "I can't sign it without the readings. People's health matters more than our bonus." He added the numbers and sent the report up.
The inspection came. The bonus went. For weeks, colleagues barely spoke to him.
Mohit felt lonely, but steady. "I don't think I'm better than anyone," he told his father. "I just couldn't live with it."

qa.q: How many leak readings were left out?
qa.a: Two leak readings.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling the night he couldn't eat?
qa.a: He felt troubled and anxious, thinking about the villagers downstream who used the canal water.

qa.q: What did Mohit choose, and what did it cost him?
qa.a: He added the missing readings and sent the report up; he lost the bonus and was shunned by colleagues for weeks.

qa.q: How might the villagers downstream be affected by Mohit's choice?
qa.a: The inspection could protect their water and health, even though they might never know who spoke up.

grounding: It shows an adult acting on a principle of human welfare against the group's wishes and accepting the cost.

passage:
Dear Farida,
You'll hear it from Ammi, so I wanted you to hear it from me first. I've resigned from the housing society committee.
Last week they voted to stop renting flats to unmarried couples and to "certain communities". They said it was about "keeping the society peaceful". Eleven votes to one. Mine.
I argued. I said every person deserves a home and respect, whatever their faith or their life. Nobody listened. Some called me naïve.
It's their rule now. I can't stop them. But I won't put my name on it.
I know this costs me. Uncle Hamid won't speak to me. Ammi is worried about what neighbours will say.
I'm not sure I'm always this brave. Most days I'm not. But on this one, I couldn't bend.
Pankaj

qa.q: How many votes were cast in favour of the new rule?
qa.a: Eleven votes.

qa.q: How does Pankaj feel about resigning?
qa.a: Pankaj feels firm in principle but also sad and a bit lonely, knowing the cost with family and neighbours.

qa.q: What choice did Pankaj make, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Pankaj resigned rather than put a name to a rule that denied people dignity, acting on principle even though the group disagreed.

qa.q: How might the families the rule shuts out feel if they knew someone objected?
qa.a: They might feel a little less alone and more respected, knowing one person stood up for them.

grounding: It shows an adult acting on principles of dignity against a group's rule and accepting the personal cost.

"You want to know why I left the company? I'm Raghav. I was a junior engineer at a chemical plant.
My manager told me to sign off a waste report that said the water going into the river was clean. It wasn't. I'd tested it myself. The village downstream, where Alka's family lives, uses that river.
Everyone said, 'Just sign. It's normal. Everyone does it. You'll lose your job.' Even my father said it.
I lay awake. I kept asking myself, what if it were my own family drinking that water? Their dignity, their health, isn't less than mine.
So I didn't sign. I reported it properly to the pollution control board. I lost my job. It took me eight months to find another.
I don't think I'm some saint. Most days I'm just ordinary. But on that one thing, I couldn't bend."

qa.q: Whose family lives in the village downstream?
qa.a: Alka's family lives there.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling as he lay awake?
qa.a: Raghav felt torn and troubled, weighing the pressure to sign against the dignity and health of the people downstream.

qa.q: What choice did Raghav make, and what did it cost?
qa.a: He refused to sign the false report and reported it properly to the pollution control board, losing his job for eight months.

qa.q: How might Alka's family be affected by Raghav's choice?
qa.a: They might be protected from unsafe water, even though they may never know who spoke up.

grounding: An adult acts on self-chosen principles of human dignity against group pressure and accepts the cost, while claiming to be ordinary most days.

passage:
January: Farida, a young lawyer in Mumbai, joined a big firm. She followed all the rules and liked the respect.
April: Her senior asked her to hide documents that showed a client's factory had underpaid women workers for years. Everyone on the team said, "It's how the firm protects clients." Swati, her friend in the firm, said, "Don't be naive. It's legal enough."
Farida couldn't sleep. She thought of the women on the factory line. Their dignity mattered as much as anyone's.
June: Farida refused and reported the matter through the Bar Council's formal complaint process. She was asked to leave the firm. She now works at a small legal aid office, earning much less.
"Do you regret it?" Swati asked.
"Some days. But not the choice."

qa.q: What did the hidden documents show?
qa.a: That a client's factory had underpaid women workers for years.

qa.q: How did Farida feel about the request to hide documents?
qa.a: She was deeply troubled and couldn't sleep, feeling the workers' dignity mattered as much as anyone's.

qa.q: What choice did Farida make, and what did it cost her?
qa.a: She refused and reported it formally, losing her place at the firm and now earning much less.

qa.q: How does Swati see Farida's choice?
qa.a: Swati first calls her naive, then asks if she regrets it, seeming unsure but curious.

grounding: Over months, a young lawyer acts on principles of justice and dignity against her team and accepts the cost, still feeling some regret.

passage:
"Devika, you asked about the bravest thing I ever did. Your Momo-la, your grandmother, will tell you, but it wasn't brave the way films show.
I, Tenzin, was twenty-five, a teacher at a village school in Himachal. The headmaster made a rule: children from the labourers' camp couldn't sit with the other children. Most of the teachers agreed. Parents agreed. It was 'how things are'.
I didn't sleep for three nights. Every child sitting on that floor was as much a person as my own nieces.
So I sat those children with the others in my class. I told the headmaster why, and I wrote to the education office. I was transferred to a far school for two years.
I'm not a saint, beta. I've been petty and scared plenty of times. But that one time, I knew what I believed."

qa.q: How long was Tenzin transferred to a far school?
qa.a: For two years.

qa.q: How did young Tenzin feel during the three sleepless nights?
qa.a: She felt troubled and torn, knowing every child mattered as much as her own nieces, while everyone else accepted the rule.

qa.q: What choice did Tenzin make, and what did it cost her?
qa.a: She seated the camp children with the others, explained why and wrote to the education office, and was transferred far away for two years.

qa.q: How might the labourers' children have felt sitting with the others?
qa.a: They likely felt seen and respected, perhaps for the first time in that school.

grounding: An elder recalls acting on the principle of every child's dignity against a school rule and accepting the cost, while calling herself ordinary.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: The rain had flooded the Gurgaon underpass, and it was nearly eleven when Jaya arrived at the women's hostel with two suitcases and a booking confirmation. Mahima, the night manager, checked the list. Beside the name was a note from the owners in red: 'Northeast. Refuse politely.' The owners had made it a rule, and the other staff went along. Mahima looked at Jaya, soaked, holding a phone at one per cent. A person's home state was not a reason to leave her on a flooded road; Mahima was sure of that. She gave Jaya a room, wrote in the log exactly what she had done and why, and emailed the owners that night. The next week they cut her bonus and moved her to day shifts. She kept the log entry. She didn't regret it.

qa.q: What did the owners' note in red say?
qa.a: 'Northeast. Refuse politely.'

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling as she looked at Jaya?
qa.a: Mahima felt a firm, uneasy conviction that the rule was wrong, moved by Jaya standing soaked with a dying phone.

qa.q: Why did Mahima write in the log exactly what she did and why?
qa.a: Being open about refusing the owners' rule showed she was acting on principle, not hiding, and was ready to accept the cost.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel being given a room that night?
qa.a: Jaya would feel relieved and safe, and, if she ever learned of the note, grateful to be treated as a person rather than a label.

grounding: A young manager refuses a discriminatory rule her employers and coworkers accept, acts openly and bears the cost.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage: The file on Pankaj's desk at the Mumbai ward office needed one more signature: clearance of the pavement shelters along the nala, with twenty-four hours' notice, in the middle of July rain. Everyone else had signed. His senior, Sachin, leaned on the desk. 'It's procedure, Pankaj. Upstairs wants it done. Don't be a hero.' Pankaj thought of the woman who sold vadas under a blue tarp there, her two children doing homework by torchlight. Forty families, and nowhere arranged for them to go. He did not tear the file or leak it. He wrote a signed dissent: removal without shelter in the monsoon went against the dignity the rules were meant to protect. Then he sent it up with the file. The clearance was delayed a month while shelter was found. In October Pankaj was transferred to the stores department.

qa.q: How many families lived in the pavement shelters?
qa.a: Forty families.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when Sachin said 'Don't be a hero'?
qa.a: Pankaj felt pressured but troubled in conscience, unable to forget the vada seller and her children under the tarp.

qa.q: Why is a signed dissent a principled choice here?
qa.a: It states the objection openly on the record, without tearing or leaking the file, and accepts the consequences instead of hiding.

qa.q: How might Sachin see Pankaj's dissent?
qa.a: Sachin probably sees it as naive trouble-making that complicates procedure, since everyone else had signed.

grounding: A young official acts on a principle of dignity against his whole office's decision, openly, and accepts a transfer as the cost.

'The panchayat voted, Sunaina. Seven to two. The new cook goes, or the parents pull the children out.'
'Because she's from the wrong caste.'
'They didn't say that.'
'Mohit, they didn't need to.' Sunaina kept packing her school bag. 'She cooks clean, she cooks well, and the children love her dal. Tomorrow I eat her food with them, on the same mat.'
'They'll complain to the block office. You could lose the posting.'
'Then I lose it.' Her voice shook a little. 'I've taught these kids every morning that people are equal. What am I, if I don't mean it at lunch?'
'And if nobody else stands with you?'
'Then I write to the education officer and stand alone. But openly, with my name.'
Mohit sat down heavily. 'I'll drive you in tomorrow,' he said at last.

qa.q: How did the panchayat vote?
qa.a: Seven to two.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's shaking voice suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Sunaina felt afraid of the cost, even while staying determined to act on her belief in equality.

qa.q: What makes Sunaina's plan a principled stand rather than plain defiance?
qa.a: She acts openly under her own name, writes to the education officer, and is ready to lose the posting, all for the cook's dignity.

qa.q: How might the cook feel if she learns Sunaina ate with her on the same mat?
qa.a: The cook would likely feel respected and less alone, seeing someone publicly refuse to treat her as lesser.

grounding: A young teacher stands by a principle of equal dignity against the village majority, openly and ready to pay the price.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Last Christmas season the hotel in Goa was full to the roof, and the manager called me aside. "Yusuf, if guests from that one community come asking, say we're booked. Other guests complain." Yash, at the next counter, just nodded. Everyone did.
I couldn't. That night a family came in, tired kids asleep on their shoulders, and we had rooms. I gave them one. Next morning I told the manager, calmly, that I would not turn people away for who they are, and that he could write me up if he wanted.
He did. I lost my festival bonus and was moved to night shifts for two months. Yash said I was mad.
I'm not a saint. I've kept quiet about smaller things before, and probably will again. But that one, I couldn't carry.

qa.q: What did it cost Yusuf to give the family a room?
qa.a: Yusuf lost the festival bonus and was moved to night shifts for two months.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel about turning people away, and what shows it?
qa.a: Yusuf felt it was deeply wrong, something impossible to carry, so stayed calm and firm even knowing a write-up would follow.

qa.q: Which parts of Yusuf's response would you point out to someone facing an unfair instruction?
qa.a: Yusuf acted openly and calmly, told the manager directly, and accepted the consequences instead of hiding or lying about it.

qa.q: Why might Yash react differently?
qa.a: Yash, like everyone else, went along with the manager, perhaps valuing the job and the group's approval more, so Yusuf's stand looked mad to Yash.

grounding: An adult refuses a discriminatory instruction on principle, accepts the cost, and admits not always living up to it.
